omer.voice_hint: Omer as an adult narrator: Israeli man, late 30s. Warm, slightly raspy, a little smoky, light Israeli accent in English, dry humor, laughs at himself. Real, unpolished and conversational, like telling a story to a friend at 1 a.m. NOT an announcer, trailer or audiobook voice. Hebrew words (Modiin, savta, Bissli, dugri, chutzpah, Tzofim, madrich, Yom HaZikaron, matkot, Technion, Bamba) said natively.
omer.style_notes: Wry, relaxed, laughs at himself. A memory, never a pitch. About 140 to 150 words per minute. Slow way down and go almost to a whisper for the siren and Yom HaZikaron shots, and for the last three lines.

shira.voice_hint: Shira as an adult narrator: Israeli woman, late 30s, grew up on a kibbutz. Low-ish warm voice, light Israeli accent in English, direct and funny, a little husky. Real, unpolished and conversational, like telling a story to a friend. NOT an announcer, trailer or audiobook voice. Hebrew words (kibbutz, Dalia, dugri, Yom HaZikaron, achi, tachles, Bamba) said natively.
shira.style_notes: Dry, direct, warm underneath. A memory, never a pitch. About 140 to 150 words per minute. Slow way down and go almost to a whisper for the siren and Yom HaZikaron shots, and for the last three lines.

style_notes: A memory, never a pitch. Talk, don't announce, about 140 to 150 words per minute. Lift into the jokes, slow way down for the sirens and Yom HaZikaron (almost a whisper there), and for the last three lines. Each line has a 'path': the viewer picks Omer or Shira at the start and only hears that path's lines. Childhood shots only exist in their own path; shared shots (06-draft onward) have one line set per path. Audio tags are ElevenLabs v3 tags; drop them if the model reads them aloud. 'at' is seconds from the moment that shot starts. Gaps are on purpose: the in-scene character lines in shots.json are timed to land in them, the same for both paths. Lines can run past the end of a clip, so hold or loop the clip while they finish. Duck clip audio about 8 dB under narration. Shot 'ending' is the closing section after 17-mentor (company cards, stats, the Musk quote). 'shot_seconds' = how long each shot must stay on screen on each path so its narration finishes; hold or loop the clip until then. Hard numbers live in the site's margin notes, so the narration only carries the ones that feel lived.

lines.text: [softly] I grew up in Modiin. White stone, parks, too many roundabouts.
Honestly? Our company started way before the company.
Rinat loved that question. My mom calls it chutzpah. [laughs] Not always as a compliment.
One toss. I got one toss. [laughs] Nobody was offended. That's dugri. You just say the thing.
Summers at my savta's in Sderot.
You get about fifteen seconds. I counted once. I got to nine.
Inside, Bissli and cards. I held my cousin's hand like I wasn't scared.
Then the door opened...
[laughs] and we went right back outside.
[softly] On Yom HaZikaron, the whole country stops. Two minutes. People get out of their cars and just stand there.
My dad didn't say a word. In six years, it would be me.
Fifteen, a madrich in the Tzofim. Managing people before I could drive.
Eighteen. Almost everyone goes. Thirty-two months for me.
[softly] I walked right past her. No idea.
Combat basic. Three a.m., a stretcher, my whole squad under it.
You learn you can keep going way past quitting. And that nobody finishes alone.
Up north, a kibbutz girl I hadn't met was getting into eighty-two hundred. Cyber. Intelligence.
Nineteen, three a.m., running a live system. Her friends abroad were picking majors.
Me? Golan Heights. Tech guy for a tank crew.
Something's dead before a dawn exercise, and it's on you.
Dawn briefing on the hood of a jeep.
Way lower rank. He handed me the marker anyway.
Her unit debriefed everything. Say it, fix it, move on.
Those people became her cofounders and investors. The four Wiz founders came out of eighty-two hundred together too.
After the army, about a third of us just leave. South America. Matkot, obviously.
No money, no plan. You get good at improvising.
Then the Technion. And one weekend, a hackathon in Tel Aviv.
[laughs] I argued with a girl from the other team for an hour. By morning we'd merged teams. That was Shira.

Twenty-seven. Me, Shira, Noam, Lena, one tiny apartment. The money was there partly thanks to Yozma. In nineteen ninety-three the government put a hundred million dollars into ten venture funds and basically started an industry.
Our first company died. [sighs] Beach till two a.m.
Here, failing isn't the end of you. A World Economic Forum report says Israel accepts it more than anywhere. So we went again.
Round two worked.
[excited] One text, and the office lost its mind. We weren't the first. We won't be the last.
Shira mentors kids now. I bring the Bamba.
[softly] Six-year-old me would have loved her.
There's no single reason. A kid here just spends twenty years practicing to be a founder before ever starting a company.
Elon Musk said it once, and my mom won't stop quoting it. Innovation per capita, Israel must be number one by far in the world.
[softly] Me? I'm still the kid asking why.
[warmly] I was born on a kibbutz up north. Cows, orchards, a water tower, and about four hundred people who all thought they could raise me. [laughs] Tachles? They were right.

I was six. Dalia was explaining something about cows and water, and it didn't add up. So I screamed... [shouting] WHY? [beat] I wasn't scared. [firmly] In Israel, people aren't afraid to speak up when something isn't right. [warmly] We call it chutzpah.
[laughs] On a kibbutz, everyone argues about everything. So at nine, I stood on a bench and told the whole room they were wrong. [beat] In Israel, you just say it straight.
[softly] Ten years old, at the pool. Then the siren. [beat] I didn't freeze. I grabbed the little kid next to me and ran. In Israel, you learn that before you learn two plus two.
[softly] Inside, it was hot and crowded, and someone always had cards. We played and waited for the boom. [firmly] Survival mode is instilled very early on.

[softly] [sad] Once a year, the whole country stops. Even the cars on the highway. [beat] I stood next to my mom and read the names. [crying] Some I knew. [softly] And I understood: in six years, it's my turn.
[laughs] At fifteen I was in charge of twelve kids and a broken irrigation line. Nobody came to fix it. [firmly] On a kibbutz, you don't wait. Yalla, you fix it yourself.
[warmly] At eighteen, almost everyone goes to the army. [firmly] From rich kids to kibbutz kids, everyone serves together.
They didn't care where I grew up. Only how I think. [excited] Unit 8200, cyber and intelligence. Israel trusts teenagers with things most countries wouldn't trust adults with.
[softly] Three in the morning. A live system, and I'm nineteen and in charge. [beat] Most people my age are partying in college. I was learning to lead when it matters.
After every mission, we sat in a circle. I told my commander the mistake was hers. She said "true" and wrote it down. [firmly] In Israel, the best idea wins, not the highest rank.

[warmly] These people became my family. My achim. We went through so much hardship together. They're my future cofounders, my first hires, my first investors. [beat] In Israel, your army unit doesn't last just three years, they're your brothers and sisters for life.

[laughs] After the army, every Israeli disappears. HaTiyul HaGadol. The big trip. [beat] So there I was above Machu Picchu, slamming shesh besh. A tourist asked where we were from. [firmly] When your country always has to defend itself, you say it proudly.
[excited] No money, no plan, a boat held together with tape, and a snake. [laughs] Total balagan. [beat] We always figured it out. That trip taught me risk isn't scary. It's how things start.

[laughs] At a hackathon in Tel Aviv, I argued with a curly-haired guy for an hour. Loudly. [beat] By morning, he said "tachles, yours is better." That's how I met Omer. In Israel, the person you fight with today can be your partner tomorrow.

[warmly] Back home, I started a company with my friend Omer. I drew a safe little circle. He drew one ten times bigger. [beat] He wasn't scared. [firmly] Israel started as a crazy dream too. Im tirtzu, ein zo agada. If you will it, it's no dream.
[softly] Our first company failed. Completely. [beat] We sat on the beach, ate garinim, and laughed about it. [firmly] In Israel, failing isn't the end. Yalla. Round two.

[excited] Years later, one phone call. [shouting] We got the exit! [laughs] The office lifted me up in a chair like it was a wedding. [warmly] We weren't the first Israelis to do this. We won't be the last.
[softly] Now I'm the one at the front of the class. [beat] And a little girl in the first row just asked why. [warmly] It starts all over again.
